headline: Paul Miron positions Msquared Capital's income fund as a consistent, low-risk private credit alternative that avoids property construction exposure
reasoning: Miron explains that investor feedback drove the fund's design: clients explicitly did not want exposure to construction, land, specialised security, or second mortgages. He characterises the fund's positioning as 'boring and consistent,' functioning well across different economic cycles. The fund is positioned as a portfolio diversifier where investors can allocate capital with confidence that it is insulated from the negative headlines around property developer collapses.
quote: We've had the open conversation and the feedback from our investors is we don't want to have exposure to that sector. If I'm investing into the income fund. So it's not only construction, it's land, it's specialised security, it's second mortgages. It's all of the things that you can get caught on in a negative economic cycle, um, where private credit or our product sits really well is that actually it's it's boring, it's consistent. And and it works really well in different cycles. So when someone wants to park money into private credit in our fund, um, you know, there's many reasons. Part of your larger portfolio. It just needs to have that consistency and transparency of knowing that when they pick up the paper in the morning and they see another property developer falling over because of market cycles, they know that their money is not exposed.
episode_title: Property downturn reveals private credit cracks

headline: Paul Miron warns private credit investors against construction and development lending as rising costs and falling end-markets make capital loss risks too high relative to extra return
reasoning: Miron has been telling clients for nearly a decade that construction lending carries risks that may not be worth the additional rate premium. He says the last four years have seen construction economics become harder than ever, with costs rising, land prices inelastic and end-market values falling around 10%, making it very difficult for developers to profit. For private credit lenders exposed to this segment, the possibility of losing capital is significantly higher, and investors need to assess whether extra yield justifies that risk. He distinguishes this from short-term income-focused lending which is more dynamic and less exposed to the underlying asset's value.
quote: Right now, in the last four years, it's been harder than it's ever been before. The economics of building or developing has never been harder. Construction costs are going high. Land is inelastic, doesn't really fall. Um, and the end market has fallen by 10% at the moment. So it's very difficult for a property developer to actually make profit on a, on a transaction. And so if you're a private credit lender and lending money to that transaction, your your possibility of a losing your capital is significantly higher. and you really need to ask yourself, is it worth the extra risk to get that extra little bit of return?
episode_title: Property downturn reveals private credit cracks

headline: Highlighted as an example of large-scale developer stress, with over $3 billion in debt and slowing property sales threatening its cash position

headline: Paul Miron expects at least 10% aggregate decline in Australian property prices, with some segments falling 15-20%, accelerated by budget policy changes
reasoning: Miron argues the Australian property market was already weakening before the federal budget, and the budget's demand-dampening measures hastened the decline. He believes the policy does not solve the housing crisis because it increases rents and reduces supply. He expects an aggregate 10% fall in property prices, with some segments potentially declining 15-20%. He sees the economics of building as harder than they have ever been, with construction costs rising, land prices inelastic, and end-market values already down around 10%.
quote: Statistically speaking, I think we're headed for at least 10% drop in aggregate property prices, meaning that some segments are going to do better. They're not going to fall as much, and some segments are going to do might even be as big as 15 or 20%. So this is something that we're seeing on the ground as a private credit provider at the moment. And we're obviously watching very closely, seeing the information, adjusting our policies in relation to what the market is.

headline: Paul Miron sees contagion risk from property development stress spreading to the broader Australian economy, given property represents 67% of national wealth and 15% of GDP
reasoning: Miron argues that while capital-loss contagion can be limited depending on which segment of private credit an investor is in, the macroeconomic contagion risk is real given property's enormous weight in Australian wealth and GDP. With property at 67% of household wealth and contributing around 15% of GDP, a slowdown has significant implications for state government tax revenues and broader economic activity. He expects the current credit cycle change to continue for another one to two years.
quote: There's risk of contagion to other property development transactions and the whole sector. Um, we need to appreciate that 67% of our wealth as Australians held in property, it's it contributes about 15% of our GDP. So that part is going to slow down. It's a big tax revenue earner for our state governments. So I think macroeconomics, yes, is a contagion in relation to losing capital. I think a lot of investors need to understand where the money is invested, what exposure they have, what segments of the private credit market they're in.
episode_title: Property downturn reveals private credit cracks
